props.title: Inspector Clouseau
props.initialSlug: Bumbling detective hunts a master thief in London

sections.content: The 1968 Inspector Clouseau marked a curious detour in the Pink Panther franchise, with Alan Arkin replacing Peter Sellers in the iconic role. This oddity sits between A Shot in the Dark (1964) and Return of the Pink Panther (1975), attempting to capitalize on the character's popularity without its defining star. Arkin's interpretation takes Clouseau in a markedly different direction - less bumbling aristocrat, more determined fool. Director Bud Yorkin aimed for a grittier tone than Blake Edwards' previous entries, resulting in a film that feels somewhat disconnected from the series' established comedy style.

sections.content: While Inspector Clouseau stumbled, it inadvertently highlighted what made Sellers' portrayal so special. His absence proved how crucial his physical comedy and accent work were to the character's appeal. The film's attempt at a more serious crime plot involving counterfeit money showed why the franchise worked best when embracing pure comedy. When Sellers returned in The Return of the Pink Panther (1975), he immediately restored the character's essential charm, leading to three more successful entries including The Pink Panther Strikes Again (1976). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

The Clouseau character's influence extends far beyond this 1968 misfire. The bumbling detective archetype it helped popularize can be seen in everything from Johnny English (2003) to The Naked Gun (1988). Steve Martin's attempt to reboot the franchise with The Pink Panther (2006) and The Pink Panther 2 (2009) proved again how difficult it was to step into Sellers' shoes. The original series' impact on comedy can't be overstated - its blend of sophistication and slapstick influenced countless films including Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery (1997) and OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies (2006).
